transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-02-12 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Location: Zoom / Fireflies recording
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Miguel Santos (Redwood SE), Priya Sharma (Acme Head of AI), Mark Chen (Acme Platform Engineer), Aisha Brown (Acme SecOps)

Summary:
- Redwood demo focused on structured output and function/tool-calling (referred to in the call as JSON mode, schemas, and guardrails).
- Discussed API usage patterns, Console tools for schema wiring, and Redwood Optimize recommendations to balance latency/cost for structured outputs.
- Agreed next steps: share demo notebook, pricing, and schedule an in-house POC benchmark.

Topics:
- JSON mode / structured output schemas
- Function / tool calling & guardrails (validation, fallback)
- Console walkthrough: routes, policies, schema registry
- Optimize recommendations: batching, quantization profiles, model variants for accuracy vs cost
- Security questions: KMS, VPC/private deployment, audit logs

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro — I'm Lena on the account team, and Miguel is our SE. We planned a tight 45 minute demo to show JSON mode structured outputs, and how the Console ties into tool/function calling and Optimize.
[00:18] Miguel (SE): Hi all. super excited. Priya, Mark, Aisha — anything specific you want to get to?
[00:25] Priya (Customer): Yeah, hi — thanks. We're evaluating how to get deterministic structured responses from models for our checkout workflows, and also call internal pricing service as a tool. So, main questions: can we enforce a schema, validate responses, and safely call internal services? Also curious about per-call latency impact.
[00:42] Miguel (SE): Great. We'll show the API JSON mode — where you pass a schema like a JSON Schema and the model returns a validated JSON object, plus how you can wire tool caps to call internal endpoints. There are guardrails around validation failures and fallbacks.
[01:05] Mark (Customer): Do you have an example of fallback? If the model returns malformed json, what happens?
[01:12] Miguel (SE): Yes. We show two patterns: 1) strict mode — the request fails with a schema validation error and we return a structured error to your app; 2) tolerant mode — Redwood attempts a repair pass (another short completion, often costs tiny extra tokens) or routes to a fallback model variant. We'll demo both.
[01:32] Aisha (Customer): And from a security standpoint, how are tool calls authenticated? We can't just have the model call out unauthenticated.
[01:40] Lena (AE): Good callout. We support short-lived signed tokens for tool calls, VPC egress controls on Private/Dedicated, and you can restrict what endpoints are callable via a policy in the Console. We'll show that in the Console walkthrough.
[01:55] Miguel (SE): Alright jumping into the API demo. (shares screen) Here's a sample request. We'll use JSON mode with a schema that expects {"price": number, "currency": string, "discount_applied": boolean}.
[02:12] Miguel (SE): (typing) POST /v1/generate?mode=json
Headers: Authorization: Bearer <redacted>
Body: prompt: 'Calculate final price given base price 35.00 and coupon SPRING10'
schema: {"type": "object", "properties": {"price": {"type": "number"}, "currency": {"type": "string"}, "discount_applied": {"type": "boolean"}}, "required": ["price", "currency"] }
[02:50] Miguel (SE): Sending the request... response comes back as a JSON object; Redwood validates it server-side against the schema and returns either the object or an error payload.
[03:05] (short pause, typing)
[03:20] Miguel (SE): Here's a case where the model returned something like "35 dollars" for price. Redwood detects type mismatch (string vs number), and in strict mode it returns error code "schema_mismatch" along with the raw model output. In tolerant mode it tries a repair step: we set up a small, cheap auto-correct pass that converts "35 dollars" to 35.0 and re-validate.
[03:45] Priya (Customer): That repair pass—does it count as additional tokens/charges?
[03:50] Miguel (SE): Yes it does, but it's minimal. We also have Optimize suggestions to reduce those edge cases—like a small prompt template and constrained model variant to reduce repair frequency.
[04:05] Lena (AE): Quick architecture note — in Dedicated/Private you can run the entire validation and repair in your VPC; for Hosted we do the validation in our control plane but you can encrypt payloads with your KMS and we keep audit logs.
[04:25] Aisha (Customer): Audit logs — are they token-level or only request-level? We need traceability for PCI-type flows.
[04:32] Lena (AE): We capture request/response hashes, timestamps, model variant, route, and policy decisions. Full payload retention is configurable; we can turn on extended retention under an enterprise package.
[04:45] Miguel (SE): Now switching to Console — here's the Schema Registry. You can register named schemas, version them, and reference them by route.
[05:02] (screen: Redwood Console - Schemas)
[05:10] Miguel (SE): I'll attach the schema to a route called /pricing/finalize and enable strict=false, repair=true, fallback_model: small-variant-4bit. Also we can attach a tool binding "pricing_service_v1" that maps to an internal endpoint https://acme-svc/pricing/calc with an allowlist.
[05:35] Mark (Customer): When you say allowlist, that's enforced where? At Redwood runtime?
[05:40] Miguel (SE): Correct — enforced at the runtime that runs the tool call. For Private, that's customer-hosted runtime so policy enforcement stays in your network boundary.
[05:52] Priya (Customer): You mentioned function calling — is that the same as tool calling here?
[05:58] Miguel (SE): They overlap. We support a function-calling style where the model returns a function name + args (like the OpenAI schema), and we also support a direct tool call where Redwood can automatically call your endpoint using the structured args. In both cases we validate the args against the registered schema and apply guardrails.
[06:18] (few seconds of typing)
[06:30] Miguel (SE): Now I'll demo a live run that hits a small hosted test model. (sends) Timestamped output: [06:45] Response returned in 320ms: {"price": 31.5, "currency": "USD", "discount_applied": true} — validated OK.
[06:58] Priya (Customer): 320ms is great. What model was that?
[07:02] Miguel (SE): We used a lower-cost small-variant on the hosted catalog for this example. Optimize will recommend a model based on your latency and cost SLOs.
[07:12] Lena (AE): For production we typically recommend a small POC on Dedicated to measure steady-state request QPS and to tune batching.
[07:20] Mark (Customer): Speaking of batching — if we batch multiple structured requests, does validation happen per-item?
[07:26] Miguel (SE): Yes per-item. Batching is token-level batching for throughput; we validate each item individually and report per-item success/failure. The Console shows per-route token breakdown and repair counts.
[07:40] Priya (Customer): Can we set guardrails that route complex cases to a human-in-the-loop? e.g., if the repair confidence is low.
[07:48] Miguel (SE): Absolutely. You can define policy rules that when confidence < 0.6 route to a webhook or mark for manual review, and the Console will tag those traces.
[08:00] Aisha (Customer): On encryption — you said KMS; do you support customer KMS keys?
[08:05] Lena (AE): Yes we integrate with AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and HSMs for Private deployments. For Hosted you can bring your own keys for payload encryption at rest.
[08:15] (short pause)
[08:30] Miguel (SE): Now I'll show tool calling flow. I'll trigger a prompt that asks the model to call the pricing_service_v1 tool. The model returns function args: {"product_id": "SKU-123", "qty": 3}. Redwood validates and then signs a short-lived token and makes the POST to the allowlisted endpoint.
[08:58] (typing)
[09:10] Miguel (SE): Response came back: {"final_price": 95.0, "currency": "USD"}. The Console logs show the endpoint return, latency, and correlation id.
[09:25] Mark (Customer): Are the tool calls proxied or do you allow direct egress from a customer Private runtime?
[09:32] Miguel (SE): For Hosted, calls are proxied through Redwood with signed tokens. For Private runtimes, they can call your internal endpoints directly in your VPC—no egress to Redwood control plane needed.
[09:45] Priya (Customer): What about model hallucination when generating args intended for tools—do you validate allowed keys or types?
[09:52] Miguel (SE): Yes, the schema registry enforces allowed properties and types. If the model returns an unexpected field, the runtime drops it and logs it, or you can configure to fail the call.
[10:05] (laughter)
[10:12] Priya (Customer): Good. Next, can you show how Optimize recommends quantization vs latency tradeoffs for structured outputs?
[10:20] Miguel (SE): Sure. Optimize uses your route telemetry—latency percentiles, repair counts, token cost—and suggests quantization levels and batching windows. For example, it might recommend int8 quantization on a large model and a 50ms batching window to get 20% cost savings while keeping p95 below 400ms.
[10:42] Miguel (SE): (shares Optimize dashboard) Here we have a rule: if repair_rate > 2% recommend prompt tightening + switch to small-variant for non-critical routes.
[10:55] Priya (Customer): Can Optimize do automated A/B — like route 20% to a non-quantized model to check quality?
[11:02] Miguel (SE): Yes — Console supports rollout policies with canary/A-B and automatic rollback based on quality metrics tied to your evaluation prompts.
[11:12] Mark (Customer): About evals — do you host them or do we run them?
[11:17] Miguel (SE): Both. We can host eval result storage and dashboards as part of the product; customers can also run local evals and upload results. Redwood ties those evals to alerting for regressions.
[11:28] Priya (Customer): Security review question — SOC2/ISO evidence?
[11:32] Lena (AE): We have SOC2 Type II and ISO/IEC attestation documents. We'll share the security pack. For Private deployments, additional compliance options available.
[11:42] Aisha (Customer): Any customers running this exact pattern — structured outputs + tool calling — in production?
[11:47] Miguel (SE): Yes, several fintech and commerce customers use the JSON mode + tool bindings for workflows like loan calc and dynamic pricing. They'll often run Dedicated for consistent latency and private routing.
[11:59] (quick demo: intentionally malformed output)
[12:10] Miguel (SE): Now I'll force a malformed model response to show repair and fallback. (sends) Response returned as string: "thirty one point five usd" for the price field. Console shows schema_mismatch, repair attempted, repair succeeded after 2nd pass.
[12:28] Priya (Customer): Can you surface those repair traces to our S3/audit store?
[12:33] Lena (AE): Yes — audit hooks let you stream traces to your logging bucket or SIEM.
[12:40] Mark (Customer): About pricing — how do you charge for repair passes and tool calls?
[12:45] Lena (AE): Tool calls are charged as outbound API call units plus any model tokens consumed. Repair passes count as additional generation tokens. We'll include example cost calc in the pricing sheet.
[12:58] Priya (Customer): For POC we want to measure p95 latency, cost per transaction, and repair rate on our sample prompts.
[13:05] Miguel (SE): Perfect — propose week-of Feb 24 for a 2-week POC: we'll deploy a small Dedicated pool or Private runtime in your staging VPC, run 10k synthetic transactions, and produce a report.
[13:20] Priya (Customer): Sounds good. Who will own the infra setup?
[13:25] Mark (Customer): We'll own the VPC and provide short-lived creds, but Redwood will provide the deployment manifests.
[13:32] Lena (AE): We'll put that in the next steps.
[13:35] (few minutes: questions on rate limits, quotas)
[16:00] Aisha (Customer): Are there RBAC controls for who can add schemas or change route policies?
[16:06] Miguel (SE): Yes, RBAC in Console — you can limit schema registry writes to admins and tie actions to SSO groups.
[16:15] Priya (Customer): Last question on dev flow—what does local testing look like?
[16:20] Miguel (SE): We provide an SDK and a demo notebook that simulates the service (local stub) and validates outputs against the schema before you hit Redwood. We'll share the notebook.
[16:30] Lena (AE): Ok wrapping up — quick recap and next steps.
[16:35] Lena (AE): Actions: I will send pricing and the security pack; Miguel will share the demo notebook + schema examples; Priya will supply a prompt set and a target schema; Mark will provision the VPC test creds. We'll aim to kick off POC week of Feb 24.
[16:55] Priya (Customer): Thanks — very helpful. We'll look for the docs and notebook.
[17:00] Miguel (SE): Thanks everyone. Follow-up items in the recording.
[17:05] (call ends)
